Commentary.Commentary: We are all set for the chase to begin. Laura Wolvaardt has walked out in the middle with Sune Luus to open for South Africa Women. Spin straightaway as Sadia Iqbal will be bowling the first over for Pakistan Women.
... The Run Chase ...

Mid-innings Pitch Report from Sana Mir - She notes the conditions have not changed much but says there is plenty of spin on offer. She points out that Pakistan have around 16 overs of spin at their disposal and references the way Mlaba bowled as the blueprint. She stresses that bowling on those lengths will be the key to Pakistan finding success with the ball.

Shabnim Ismail, SA pacer - On the surface, Ismail notes it was a completely different wicket compared to the Australia game. She credits Marizanne Kapp's powerplay bowling for setting the tone and giving South Africa the momentum they needed. On coming back from retirement, she says it feels surreal and she is still processing being back. Says she is loving every moment of being out there with the girls in the green and gold.  About Pakistan's batting, she singles out Fana for praise, calling her contribution towards the end excellent. She is honest about what could have been done differently during Pakistan's fightback. She says they should have gone to their slower balls much quicker and that the bowlers who came on at the death could have read the wicket a bit faster and adjusted their plans accordingly. On what South Africa need to do to get over the line, she says it comes back to backing their skills. Admits that the first game did not go their way, but the message is simple in the ground. Stresses that the batters need to put their heads down and get the job done. She backs them to do it on a wicket like this, even if it will not be easy.

Kapp inspires disciplinary Proteas attack - The Proteas' bowling performance was nothing short of exceptional, brilliantly orchestrated by Marizanne Kapp, who took wickets at will to finish with stellar figures of 3 for 23. Shabnim Ismail and Ayabonga Khaka supported the pace barrage perfectly, picking up one wicket apiece to keep the pressure mounting on the batters. Interestingly, it was not a happy hunting day for the South African spin contingent, who went entirely wicketless on the slow surface, leaving the seamers to do all the damage. At one point, Pakistan were 50 for 8 but the Asian side fought hard and have ended up with 126 for 9.

Lifeline partnership rescues tottering innings - South Africa's relentless bowling attack refused to let any meaningful partnerships brew, consistently breaking through whenever Pakistan attempted to rebuild. A visibly frustrated Fatima Sana watched her batting order crumble from the non-striker's end, and at one point, it looked highly unlikely that Pakistan would even play out their full quota of 20 overs. However, a resilient ninth-wicket stand between the skipper and Tuba Hassan provided a critical lifeline, pushing the team toward the 120-run mark to help them bat through the overs and give their bowlers something to fight for. Sana top-scored with an unbeaten half-century, while Tuba batted well for her 23.

Disastrous Powerplay leaves Pakistan pinned - Pakistan Women's team endured a nightmare outing with the bat, as despite a fightback from Fatima Sana and Tuba Hassan, they posted 126 on the board. After confidently electing to bat first, Pakistani skipper Fatima Sana would never have envisioned such a dismal performance from her side. The innings simply never got off the ground, as South African speedster Marizanne Kapp struck on the very first ball of the match and claimed two wickets in an explosive opening over. From that early double-blow onward, the Asian side found themselves completely pinned to the wall, unable to recover from the initial shock.

FOUR! What a finish. 19 runs from the final over. Pakistan Women finish at 126/9! Short and wide of off, Fatima comes down the track and slashes it hard and uppishly, behind point for a boundary to finish off in style. From 50/8, this has been an insane recovery by Pakistan Women and will give them a lot of motivation.

Aliya Riaz is the next batter in.

OUT! RAMEEN SHAMIM IS RUN OUT! A complete communication lapse between the batters. That's the last thing Pakistan would have wanted. Pitched fuller and around the off stump line with a little bit of an away shape. Iram Javed nails the cover drive to the left of the mid off fielder. The fielder, Nadine De Klerk is quick to get across. First misfields but is quick to recover, and sees the chaos on the pitch. Iram wants a single and is more than halfway through, but Shamim is caught ball-watching at the non-striker's end. By the time she starts to run to the batting end, De Klerk gets rid of the ball, throwing it on the bounce to Sinalo Jafta. Rameen is forced to put in a desperate dive, but Jafta is quick to whip the bails off before the batter makes her ground. A needless throw of a wicket and Pakistan have now lost half their side in just 5.4 overs. They are 29/5.

Commentary.Commentary: The anthems are sung/chanted proudly. It is now time for game number 11 to get underway in Birmingham. The overhead conditions are fairly overcast, but there is no rain in the forecast, but as they say, when in the UK, you can't rule the rain out at all. So let's hope there is no interruption. Landmark day for Laura Wolvaardt, as she becomes the sixth South African player to feature in 100 T20I matches - informs Raunak Kapoor on air. She leads the team huddle before the Proteas spread out to take their spots on the field. Gull Feroza and Muneeba Ali are the two Pakistani openers. Marizanne Kapp has the new ball and is raring to go. Muneeba to face the firt ball. A slip in place. 3... 2... 1 and here we go!

Time for the national anthems - Wonderful, bone-chilling scenes at Edgbaston as the giant flags of both countries are unfurled in the middle. The match officials stroll out and right after them, both the captains lead their respective teams out to the middle for the anthems. It will be Pakistan's first, followed by South Africa's.

A quick word from Pakistan's opener - Muneeba Ali admits that it was a tough loss against India, but they discussed a lot during the two-day break about what needs to be done on this surface. On how the pitch played that day, she explains they were batting in the fourth innings of the day, with two matches already played on it, so it was naturally slow by then. She notes the ball was coming on nicely early but slowed considerably once the spinners got involved. Today, being the first match on this surface, she expects it to play a bit better. On bouncing back, she keeps it simple and says that is exactly what they are here for, and they will give everything in this game.

Let's hear it from the South African stalwart - Marizanne Kapp, on the loss to Australia, says the biggest thing is not to panic. She notes South Africa have been in this situation before, and the key message within the group has been to stay calm, trust their processes and keep moving forward with everything still to play for. On bowling alongside Shabnim Ismail, she says it has been great to be back operating together. Admits that the first game did not go the way they wanted, but with more matches ahead, she is hopeful they can find their rhythm and take more wickets in the Powerplay. On facing Pakistan, she says the big thing with them is you never quite know which version of the team turns up. She admits that they have some outstanding players, pointing to their captain as a standout, and expects it to be far from easy. She adds that Pakistan have played at this venue before, so the conditions will not be unfamiliar to them, and South Africa will need to produce a complete performance. About her role as a senior player, she says she knows that when she is at her best, she helps the team win games. Again reiterates that it did not quite click in the first match, but she is determined to put in a strong showing tonight and make a real contribution.

PITCH REPORT - Ebony Rainford-Brent starts by noting cool conditions at around 21 degrees with a bit of cloud cover as well. About the dimensions, she points out that the square boundaries measure 55 meters and 61 meters, respectively, while the straight boundary stretches to 70 metres and the overcast sky could offer the bowlers a little assistance. Katey Martin adds that this is the fourth game on the hybrid wicket, with 150 overs already bowled on it. Mentions that the synthetic grass stitched into the surface makes it behave almost like a hockey field, offering very little variation from the first ball to the last. She expects spinners to play a big role and notes that slowing the pace down has been a much more effective approach than bowling fast on this surface.

The captain of South Africa Women - Laura Wolvaardt, on being reminded that this is her 100th WT20I, calls it a pretty special milestone, adding that representing your country 100 times is an amazing achievement and one she is thrilled to reach at a World Cup. On the loss to Australia, she notes it was a very important game for the side. She adds they tried to take as many learnings as possible from that defeat while also putting it firmly behind them, and that today feels like a completely fresh challenge they are ready to take on. About her thoughts on the surface, she reckons it looks like a pretty good wicket and that they would probably have chosen to bat first as well, given that a couple of games have already been played on it. She still expects it to offer a very good contest overall. On the team, she informs tha they are going unchanged.

The captain of Pakistan Women - Fatima Sana opts to bat first, noting that the pitch appears to be a slow batting track where her team must execute their plans more effectively. Sana believes they performed well up until the 15th over in the previous game but she also reckons that the team needs to prove themselves and significantly improve their execution during the crucial death overs.

South Africa Women (Playing XI) - Laura Wolvaardt (C), Sune Luus, Annerie Dercksen, Nadine De Klerk, Marizanne Kapp, Chloe Tryon, Kayla Reyneke, Sinalo Jafta (WK), Shabnim Ismail, Ayabonga Khaka, Nonkululeko Mlaba.

Pakistan Women (Playing XI) - Gull Feroza, Muneeba Ali (WK), Ayesha Zafar, Iram Javed (In for Tasmia Rubab), Natalia Pervaiz, Aliya Riaz, Fatima Sana (C), Rameen Shamim, Tuba Hassan (In for Saira Jabeen), Nashra Sundhu, Sadia Iqbal.

TOSS - Time for the coin flip. Both captains, Laura Wolvaardt and Fatima Sana, are out in the middle with Ian Smith leading the proceedings. Tails is the call from Sana and it lands as Tails. Pakistan Women have opted to BAT first.

Did you know? South Africa have never lost a T20 World Cup match against Pakistan. They have won in all three of their meets - in 2012, 2014 and 2020, respectively and would like to continue that unbeaten streak against the Women in Green. Whereas Pakistan have managed to win just one of their eight T20 World Cup matches.

Just in - India dominate the Dutch - The Women in Blue have put on a comprehensive team performance to outplay the Netherlands and have handed them a crushing defeat of 95 runs.  For the Dutch, the target was daunting from the moment they walked out to chase it. World Cup debutants, learning on the job, and this was a lesson that came hard and fast. Two games, two defeats, and their campaign is all but done. But then, that was always the deal for the Netherlands. Nothing to lose, everything to absorb. The experience will shape them for the future.

One-sided affairs in Leeds - Pretty much the case at Headingley. In the first game of the day, Australia streamrolled Bangladesh by restricting them to just 77 runs and chasing it in less than 10 overs. And in the clash going on right now, between India and the Netherlands, the Dutch are nowhere in the contest as the Women In Blue have handed them a target of 210 runs to chase. As per the latest reports, the Netherlands need 97 runs from the last 4 overs, with 5 wickets in hand. While we wait for the toss in this important clash, feel free to switch tabs and glance at a couple of games, including the second Test match between England and New Zealand (Day 1), at The Oval. But do make sure you come back here at 5 pm GMT for the coin flip.

Spin to win? Edgbaston has hosted three matches in this edition so far, and the surface has been whispering a clear message. Spinners have run the show, picking up 22 wickets compared to 13 by the seamers. Pakistan have already played their first game here, against India and in that, nine of their ten wickets fell to the spinners. Whereas South Africa lost eight wickets to the turning ball in Manchester. Two sides with glaring vulnerabilities against spin, and those holes will need to be plugged urgently. The venue history does not help either side's nerves. South Africa have lost three of their four matches at Edgbaston, while Pakistan have lost all five of their T20Is here. Let’s see who makes this their happy hunting ground this time around. Toss and teams to come up very shortly.

Sorting out the vulnerabilities - Both Pakistan and South Africa struggled badly with the bat in their openers, and specifically in the chase. Pakistan were bowled out for 106, South Africa just one run better at 107, both crumbling while pursuing near-identical targets. The batting needs to be considerably better from both sides here, and they know it. Pakistan's problems run deeper though. Their batting unit has simply not fired collectively, and the numbers in the chase make for grim reading. One win from their last six while chasing, and in T20 World Cups, nine defeats from ten matches batting second. That is not a rough patch. That is a pattern. Their highest successful run chase in all T20Is reads 156, and that came against South Africa of all teams. As for the Proteas, their highest successful run chase in T20 World Cup history stands at just 135, and that is despite having Wolvaardt in prime form at the top and the likes of Kapp and De Klerk to follow in the order. The talent is there. The chasing record simply does not reflect it. Something has to give, and for both these sides, it has to give today.

Pain, purpose, and redemption - Hurt has a funny way of lighting a fire. The deeper the wound, the brighter it burns. And sometimes, the heaviest defeats carry the loudest message, that the only way out is through. Two wounded sides. One shot at redemption. It is all set to happen here. Pakistan felt the full force of India's precision on Sunday, a 65-run defeat that left no room for argument. A day earlier, South Africa walked into Australia's buzzsaw and came out the other side 64 runs lighter and considerably quieter. Badly bruised from those evenings, these two sides meet each other in Birmingham with their campaigns teetering on the edge and redemption the only thing on their minds. On that note, hello and welcome to our coverage of the 11th match of the ICC Women’s T20 World Cup, 2026.
... MATCH DAY ...

Desperation rules the battle to stay alive - The stakes have dramatically escalated for Match 11 of the ICC Women's T20 World Cup 2026 at Edgbaston, as two wounded sides fight to rescue their campaigns. Both South Africa Women and Pakistan Women are seeking their first points after heavy defeats in their respective opening group-stage matches. With the race for a semi-final spot rapidly tightening in Group A, this high-pressure, mid-week clash represents a critical crossroads. Neither side can afford another misstep if they hope to keep their dreams of global silverware alive on English soil. Lethal SA seek urgent repairs - South Africa Women boast a formidable lineup capable of dismantling any opposition, yet they are feeling the heat after a 65-run opening defeat to powerhouse Australia. While the Proteas are renowned for their raw pace and explosive batting, their execution fell flat when tested by the reigning world champions. To bounce back under captain Laura Wolvaardt, the top-order must build substantial partnerships rather than leaving all the heavy lifting to the middle order. Tightening up their bowling lines and finding an extra gear in terms of tactical adaptability during the middle overs will be paramount if they intend to stamp their authority on this fixture. Erasing the open-field lapses - Pakistan Women entered the tournament with immense promise but were comprehensively outplayed by arch-rivals India in their opening fixture. The most frustrating element for Pakistan was how they let go of a highly commanding position with both bat and ball, allowing the match to slip through their fingers during critical phases. To transform their fortunes, the Women in Green must drastically improve their fielding standard to back up their hard-working bowling unit. Ground fielding leaks and dropped catches have plagued their recent outings, meaning a flawless, comprehensive team performance is needed to compete with a side as physically dominant as South Africa. Form (Last 5 completed T20Is, recent first) - SA-W - LWLWW | PAK-W - LLLWW. Opening auditions and spin squeezes - The blueprint of this game will be drawn during a couple of highly compelling individual matchups. The explosive South African opening pair of Laura Wolvaardt and Sune Luus will face an immediate examination against a highly varied Pakistan bowling attack that mixes left-arm spin with subtle pace variations. On the other hand, South African left-arm spinner Nonkululeko Mlaba will serve as the tactical key against a fragile Pakistan batting unit. If Mlaba can extract a sharp turn and exploit Pakistan's historical vulnerability against top-tier slow bowling, she can choke the scoring rates and force a cluster of middle-order errors.
